tone_statements.citation: Hajek, John. 2003. Evidence of tonal activity in Aslian. Mon-Khmer Studies 33: 59-66.
tone_statements.quote: With respect to plurisyllabic words, pitch patterns occur as follows: unstressed minor syllables bear low tone, syllables with secondary stress carry mid tone, while final syllables always bear primary stress. Three tone levels (high, mid, low) are reported to occur as follows: [...] (p. 60, reporting Phaiboon 1984) | According to the latter, pitch is contrastive, rather than predictable, but involves only two tones (high v. mid). Mid tone is considered to be the normal setting in most words, with only rare examples of high tone. (p. 62, reporting Bishop 1996) | Given the low frequency of high tone, Bishop suggests that "Kensiw is not a tonal language". But from a strictly analytical point of view, such a statement is not true. Kensiw is a tonal language, but one in which tone has very low functional yield. (p. 63)

audit.reasoning: The record codes Kensiu as fixed final stress (final stress, fixed-dominant) on the strength of a Wikipedia sentence said to summarize Bishop 1996; no source file was. I downloaded Bishop 1996 (MKS 25:227-253) from the SEAlang archive, scanned it, and found the deciding statement at p. 238 sec. 2.1: fixed, non-contrastive primary stress on the final syllable of the lexeme; minor syllables unstressed except secondary stress on the reduplicant; 'completely predictable'; backed by a preliminary acoustic check (Tumtavitikul). Sec. 3.1 (p. 240) repeats 'fixed final syllable stress.. fixed stress in multisyllabic words', including tri/tetrasyllabic Malay loans. Peterson & Bishop 2002:62 (excerpt downloaded from Internet Archive) independently restates that the major (final) syllable always has primary stress. sources.citation: Bishop, Nancy. 1996. A preliminary description of Kensiw (Maniq) phonology. Mon-Khmer Studies 25: 227-253.
sources.quote: "Kensiw has fixed, non-contrastive primary, stress which falls on the final syllable of a lexeme. In addition, minor syllables may be either completely unstressed or secondarily stressed, depending on the presence of reduplication. ... She [Tumtavitikul] found that the first syllable of a reduplicated word has secondary stress, while the last syllable receives primary stress in citation form ... the application of stress is completely predictable and, while acoustically differing, stress is not contrastive in Kensiw."
sources.locator: p. 238, sec. 2.1 Stress (p. 12); also p. 240 sec. 3.1 'fixed final syllable stress.. fixed stress in multisyllabic words'
sources.note: The primary source our Wikipedia-derived quote paraphrases; explicit stress section p. 238 confirms fixed final, non-contrastive stress. Re-cite the record to this page.

sources.citation: Matisoff, James A. 2003. Aslian: Mon-Khmer of the Malay Peninsula. Mon-Khmer Studies 33: 1-58.
sources.note: Branch-level survey: Aslian did not develop register distinctions, 'registrogenesis seems never to have occurred in this branch' (p. 13); preserved final laryngeals caused no tonal effects; no tone system described, nothing on Kensiw itself. Stress remark is Aslian-general. pp. 26-58 not searchable.

tone.quote: The final laryngeals /-h, -ʔ/, another general Mon-Khmer feature, are well preserved in Aslian, so there is no question of their engendering tonal or registral effects on the previous vowel, as in Vietnamese. ... [p. 16, fn. 69:] Perhaps this is because Aslian did not develop register distinctions, which can be demonstrated to have promoted the rampant diphthongization in such languages as Mon and Khmer.

sources.note: Not established from the abstract, which concerns phonemic aspirated voiceless stops in Thai-side Northern Aslian, their phonemic status and contact origin. Tone-relevant only as the sequel to Hajek 2003, which derives Kensiw high tone from a (possibly aspirated) voiceless onset series; Wnuk & Burenhult 2014: 975-976 treat the two papers together as 'claims of contrastive aspiration and tone in Northern Aslian (Hajek 2003, 2010)' needing reassessment. Unverified pointer.
